speaker: Unknown

zh: 在我们合作过的几百个团队之后，我们看到有一种失败模式，就是他们不知道那套基础知识是什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: Then there's this other failure mode where they never test it.
zh: 然后还有另一种失败模式，是他们从未测试过它。

en: Let's talk about the Foundation Sprint.
zh: 让我们来谈谈基础冲刺。

speaker: Unknown
en: Walk us through the process.
zh: 带我们过一遍这个过程。

speaker: Unknown
en: How does it start?
zh: 它是如何开始的？

speaker: Unknown
en: What are the steps?
zh: 有哪些步骤？

speaker: Unknown
en: The very beginning of your project, we recommend this kind of crazy idea that you clear your calendar.
zh: 在你们项目的最开始，我们推荐这种疯狂的想法，就是清空你的日历。

speaker: Unknown
en: So the core team come together for 10 hours roughly and go through a sequence of activities so that we can make all of the key decisions together.
zh: 所以核心团队聚在一起大约 10 个小时，并经历一系列活动，这样我们可以一起做出所有关键决策。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think a lot of people wonder as they're hearing this is why don't I just build something and launch it and learn?
zh: 我想很多人在听到这个时都会想，为什么我不直接构建一些东西并发布它然后学习呢？

speaker: Unknown
en: One phenomenon we've seen when teams are building things really quickly with AI is that the more AI-generated or assisted they are, the more generic they tend to turn out.
zh: 我们在团队利用 AI 构建东西非常快时观察到的一个现象是，它们越是 AI 生成或辅助的，它们往往变得越通用。

speaker: Unknown
en: Put yourself in a situation where you can slow down and do some hard thinking, some deep thinking about what's actually going to make your product unique.
zh: 把自己置于一种你可以慢下来并进行一些艰苦思考、深度思考的境地，思考到底什么会让你的产品独特。

speaker: Unknown
en: Going fast can actually slow you down in the long run.
zh: 快速行动实际上从长远来看可能会拖慢你。

speaker: Unknown
en: Today my guests are Jake Knapp and John Zeratsky.
zh: 今天我的嘉宾是 Jake Knapp 和 John Zeratsky。

speaker: Unknown
en: The framework that Jake and John share in this conversation is basically the missing manual for founders and product teams trying to refine and test their startup or product idea.
zh: Jake 和 John 在这次对话中分享的框架基本上是创始人和产品团队试图提炼和测试他们的初创公司或产品理念时的缺失手册。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's called the Foundation Sprint, and it emerged out of the famous Design Sprint, which Jake and JZ co-created, and also from working with over 300 teams, building both new product at startups and also with teams at larger companies like Google, Microsoft, YouTube, Slack, Uber, and many more.
zh: 这叫做基础冲刺，它起源于著名的设计冲刺，这是 Jake 和 JZ 共同创造的，也来自与超过 300 个团队的合作，在初创公司构建新产品，也与大公司如 Google、Microsoft、YouTube、Slack、Uber 等团队合作。

speaker: Unknown
en: They published a book with this framework at the beginning of this year called Click, and the excerpt from that book that dives into this framework is one of my most popular posts of all time and is one of the rare non-AI posts amongst the top post rankings.
zh: 他们在今年年初出版了一本包含这个框架的书叫《Click》，从那本书中深入探讨这个框架的摘录是我有史以来最受欢迎的文章之一，也是热门文章排名中罕见的非 AI 文章之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: In this conversation, make sure to get your pencils out because we go through exactly how to execute this two-day sprint, where at the end of it you have a very clear hypothesis that your entire team is aligned around that clarifies what you're building, who you're building for, how it differentiates from competitors, and how to quickly test it with real potential customers.
zh: 在这次对话中，一定要拿出你的铅笔，因为我们会确切地过一遍如何执行这个为期两天的冲刺，在结束时你会得到一个非常清晰的假设，你的整个团队都对此达成一致，它澄清了你正在构建什么，你为谁构建，它如何与竞争对手区分，以及如何用真实的潜在客户快速测试它。

speaker: Unknown
en: The two days that you invest in a sprint might be the highest ROI days in the history of your product, and I highly encourage you to do this if you're in the process of baking an idea.
zh: 你在冲刺中投入的两天可能是你产品历史上 ROI 最高的两天，如果你正在构思想法，我强烈鼓励你做这件事。

en: Many of you're building AI products, which is why I am very excited to chat with Brandon Foo, founder and CEO of Paragon.
zh: 你们很多人都在构建 AI 产品，这就是为什么我很高兴能与 Paragon 的创始人兼 CEO Brandon Foo 聊天。

speaker: Unknown
en: Hey, Brandon.
zh: 嘿，Brandon。

speaker: Unknown
en: Hey, Lenny.
zh: 嘿，Lenny。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks for having me.
zh: 谢谢你邀请我。

speaker: Unknown
en: So integrations have become a big deal for AI products.
zh: 所以集成对 AI 产品来说已经成了一件大事。

speaker: Unknown
en: Why is that?
zh: 为什么呢？

speaker: Unknown
en: Integrations are mission critical for AI for two reasons.
zh: 集成对 AI 至关重要，原因有两个。

speaker: Unknown
en: First, AI products need contacts from their customers business data, such as Google Drive files, Slack messages, or CRM records.
zh: 首先，AI 产品需要来自客户业务数据的联系，如 Google Drive 文件、Slack 消息或 CRM 记录。

speaker: Unknown
en: Second, for AI products to automate work on behalf of users, AI agents need to be able to take action across these different third-party tools.
zh: 其次，为了 AI 产品能够代表用户自动化工作，AI 智能体需要能够跨这些不同的第三方工具采取行动。

speaker: Unknown
en: So where does Paragon fit into all of this?
zh: 那么 Paragon 在这一切中处于什么位置？

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, these integrations are a pain to build, and that's why Paragon provides an embedded platform that enables engineers to ship these product integrations in just days instead of months across every use case from RAG data ingestion to agentic actions.
zh: 嗯，这些集成构建起来很痛苦，这就是为什么 Paragon 提供了一个嵌入式平台，使工程师能够在几天而不是几个月内发布这些产品集成，涵盖从 RAG 数据摄取到智能体动作的每个用例。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I know from firsthand experience that maintenance is even harder than just building it for the first time.
zh: 我根据亲身经历知道，维护甚至比第一次构建它更难。

speaker: Unknown
en: Exactly.
zh: 没错。

speaker: Unknown
en: We believe product teams should focus engineering efforts and competitive advantages, not integrations.
zh: 我们相信产品团队应该集中工程精力和竞争优势，而不是集成。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's why companies like You.com, AI21, and hundreds of others use Paragon to accelerate their integration strategy.
zh: 这就是为什么像 You.com、AI21 和数百家其他公司使用 Paragon 来加速他们的集成策略。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you want to avoid wasting months of engineering on integrations that your customers need, check out Paragon at useparagon.com/lenny.
zh: 如果你想避免在客户需要的集成上浪费数月的工程时间，请访问 useparagon.com/lenny 查看 Paragon。

speaker: Unknown
en: Jake and JZ, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
zh: Jake 和 JZ，非常感谢你们来到这里并欢迎来到播客。

speaker: Unknown
en: Hey, Lenny.
zh: 嘿，Lenny。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thanks for having us.
zh: 谢谢你的邀请。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, thanks so much for having us on again.
zh: 耶，非常感谢再次邀请我们。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is always a treat.
zh: 这总是一种享受。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is going to be a very tactical conversation.
zh: 这将是一次非常战术性的对话。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're going to be going through how to actually execute a Foundation Sprint.
zh: 我们将讨论如何实际执行 Foundation Sprint。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the reason that I'm excited to do this is you guys shared an excerpt from your book where you initially shared this whole concept.
zh: 我之所以兴奋做这件事的原因是，你们分享了你们书中的一段节选，你们最初是在那里分享这个完整概念的。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's called Click.
zh: 它叫 Click。

speaker: Unknown
en: You shared this in my newsletter and I was just looking at it, and that excerpt, that post is amongst the top 10 most popular posts of all time in my newsletter, which is especially special because it's not an AI-oriented, it's one of the few non-AI posts that are near the top 10, which just tells me how valuable this is to people.
zh: 你们在我的时事通讯里分享了它，我刚才在看它，那个节选，那篇文章是我时事通讯史上最受欢迎的前 10 篇文章之一，这特别特别，因为它不是以 AI 为导向的，它是少数几篇接近前 10 的非 AI 文章之一，这告诉我这对人们来说是多么有价值。

speaker: Unknown
en: And consistently it has sat there, it hasn't been usurped, it just continues to climb.
zh: 并且它一直稳居那里，它没有被取代，它只是持续攀升。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I'm really excited to just have a conversation where we share actually how to do this.
zh: 所以我真的很兴奋能进行一场对话，我们实际分享如何做到这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: Let me just start with the beginning, just a little backstory on how the Foundation Sprint came to be.
zh: 让我就从开始说起，只是关于 Foundation Sprint 是如何产生的少量背景故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: I know it emerged out of the now very famous Design Sprint, which you guys also developed.
zh: 我知道它源于现在非常著名的 Design Sprint，这也是你们开发的。

speaker: Unknown
en: So just give us a very brief overview of just how this came to be, this idea of this Foundation Sprint.
zh: 所以就给我们一个非常简短的概览，关于这个 Foundation Sprint 的想法是如何产生的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Well, maybe I'll start by talking about the Design Sprint part because it is essential to understanding the Foundation Sprint.
zh: 嗯，也许我可以先谈谈 Design Sprint 部分，因为它对于理解 Foundation Sprint 至关重要。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the Design Sprint first developed, I had been working at the beginning of my career at Microsoft for a few years.
zh: Design Sprint 最早开发时，我职业生涯初期在微软工作了几年。

speaker: Unknown
en: Went to Google, which is like 2007, 2008, 2009, and was working on the Gmail team, was working on some projects that were just executing well, delivering, shipping.
zh: 然后去了 Google，大概是 2007、2008、2009 年，在 Gmail 团队工作，做一些执行得很好、在交付、在发布的项目。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I had this other project, a side project that had been going on for three years with a couple of colleagues, was going nowhere, and it looked like their office was going to get shut down after the financial crisis.
zh: 但我还有另一个项目，一个和几个同事进行了三年的副业项目，正一事无成，看起来他们的办公室在金融危机后要被关闭了。

speaker: Unknown
en: They were in Stockholm.
zh: 他们在斯德哥尔摩。

speaker: Unknown
en: I went there for a week.
zh: 我去那里了一周。

speaker: Unknown
en: We cleared our calendars for the week, and we created a prototype of this, this thing because we decided, look, we're never going to get anywhere.
zh: 我们清了一周的日历，我们做了一个这个东西的原型，因为我们决定，看，我们永远不会有任何进展。

speaker: Unknown
en: We've tried making the perfect pitch.
zh: 我们尝试制作完美的推介。

speaker: Unknown
en: We've tried to make the ideal PRD, we've tried to show the ideal design, and we can't.
zh: 我们尝试制作理想的 PRD，我们尝试展示理想的设计，但我们做不到。

speaker: Unknown
en: Perfection is not working.
zh: 完美行不通。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're not able to align people, we're not able to get executive support for this thing.
zh: 我们无法统一人们的思想，我们无法为这件事获得高层的支持。

speaker: Unknown
en: We couldn't convince Larry and Sergey and Eric that they should fund this thing.
zh: 我们无法说服 Larry、Sergey 和 Eric 他们应该资助这个东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: In that week in Stockholm, we created a prototype instead.
zh: 在斯德哥尔摩的那一周，我们制作了一个原型。

speaker: Unknown
en: We decided you know what?
zh: 我们决定你知道什么？

speaker: Unknown
en: Forget it.
zh: 算了吧。

speaker: Unknown
en: We're just going to build something and put it in people's hands, put it in our fellow Googlers hands.
zh: 我们就是要把东西做出来放到人们手里，放到我们 Google 同事手里。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that prototype was what became Google Meet.
zh: 那个原型就是后来成为 Google Meet 的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: It was this video conferencing tool that you could use in the web browser.
zh: 它是一个你可以在网页浏览器中使用的视频会议工具。

speaker: Unknown
en: No big deal.
zh: 没什么大不了的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, it was really cool.
zh: 是的，真的很酷。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, the outcome of that, that's definitely probably the most productive week I've ever had.
zh: 我的意思是，那个结果，那绝对可能是我经历过最高效的一周。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the thing that struck me at the time and in hindsight was, wow, it was so different to clear the calendar for a week and have the entire focal point of every person on the team be how do we create a prototype that's so real, that works so well that people will think it's real, that they'll react like it's real, that they'll want it?
zh: 但当时和事后回想中让我震惊的是，哇，清空一周的日历，让团队里每个人的全部焦点都变成我们如何创造一个如此真实、运作得如此好的原型，让人们以为它是真的，像真的那样做出反应，他们想要它，这是如此的不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we were in survival mode.
zh: 我们处于生存模式。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were trying to keep that office from getting shut down.
zh: 我们试图阻止那个办公室被关闭。

speaker: Unknown
en: But the notion that maybe you could repeat that and recreate that is what led me to create the Design Sprint.
zh: 但也许你可以重复并重现那个过程的想法，就是导致我创造 Design Sprint 的原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: So for a couple of years at Google, I start running these one-week programs with teams trying to go at the beginning of a project from zero to a prototype at the end that we can sort of evaluate, test.
zh: 所以在 Google 的几年里，我开始用团队运行这些为期一周的项目，试图在项目开始时从零开始，到周末我们拥有的一个可以评估、测试的原型。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I went to go work at Google Ventures.
zh: 然后我去 Google Ventures 工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: So separate, one of the Alphabet companies we're investing in startups.
zh: 分开来说，这是我们投资初创公司的 Alphabet 公司之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: I meet John Zeratsky and we start running these design sprints with, well, it turned out to be over the course of five years, I don't know, couple hundred teams working in the early days with founders, in the early days of their establishing the product for the first time, trying to build it from zero to one or launching a new marketing campaign, a new ad campaign, some big high-risk endeavor.
zh: 我遇到了 John Zeratsky，我们开始运行这些设计冲刺，嗯，结果在五年里，我不知道，几百个团队，在早期与创始人一起工作，在他们首次建立产品的早期，试图从零到一构建它，或者推出一个新的营销活动，一个新的广告活动，一些大的高风险事业。

speaker: Unknown
en: We'd get to work alongside them for a week.
zh: 我们可以和他们并肩工作一周。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we ended up refining this process into a recipe.
zh: 我们最终将这个过程提炼成一个配方。

speaker: Unknown
en: So across five days, it's map, sketch, decide, prototype, and test, one big focal point for each day.
zh: 所以在五天里，是地图、草图、决定、原型和测试，每一天都有一个大的焦点。

speaker: Unknown
en: So at the end of the week, you've got a tested prototype and you learn are we on the right track or not?
zh: 所以在周末，你有一个经过测试的原型，你学到了我们是否走在正确的轨道上？

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's the Design Sprint.
zh: 这就是 Design Sprint。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's kind of the prologue, the backstory to this thing.
zh: 这算是前言，这东西的背景故事。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then after a few years at Google Ventures, John and I left and eventually together with our co-founder, Eli Blee-Goldman, we started our own venture firm, Character Capital.
zh: 然后在 Google Ventures 几年后，John 和我离开了，最终与我们的联合创始人 Eli Blee-Goldman 一起，我们创办了自己的风险投资公司，Character Capital。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's kind where the story of the Foundation Sprint comes in.
zh: 这就是 Foundation Sprint 故事开始的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: Okay, awesome.
zh: 好的，很棒。

speaker: Unknown
en: JZ, anything you wanted to add?
zh: JZ，你有什么要补充的吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: One of our goals, probably our biggest goal for starting our own VC firm was that we wanted to be able to focus on just the kinds of companies and the stage of company-building that was the most fun to us, but also was where we thought we could have the biggest impact.
zh: 我们的目标之一，大概也是我们创办自己的 VC 公司的最大目标是，我们希望能够只关注那类对我们来说最有趣的公司和公司建设阶段，但也是我们认为能产生最大影响的地方。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so for us, with our background as designers, that is the early days, the first couple of months or the first year or two years of building a new business.
zh: 所以对我们来说，凭借我们作为设计师的背景，那就是早期阶段，也就是建立新业务的前几个月或第一年或两年。

speaker: Unknown
en: And at GV, sometimes we did that, but sometimes we were working with companies that were already well established.
zh: 而在 GV，有时我们会这样做，但有时我们是在与那些已经非常成熟的公司合作。

speaker: Unknown
en: And when we'd come into those companies, they kind of knew what they were doing.
zh: 当我们进入那些公司时，他们大概知道自己在做什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: They knew what they stood for.
zh: 他们知道他们的立场是什么。

speaker: Unknown
en: They knew how they were different in the market and how they were positioned.
zh: 他们知道他们在市场上有什么不同以及他们是如何定位的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so we could help them answer these big questions and solve these problems and test their prototypes with customers.
zh: 所以我们可以帮助他们回答这些大问题并解决这些问题，并与客户一起测试他们的原型。

speaker: Unknown
